function: DDPG, TD3 and SAC agents set RIS reflection coefficients from the received pulse response, without channel estimation, to equalize ISI and boost SNR (p. 3).
system: Single-antenna BS and UE, 100-element passive reflecting ULA RIS with continuous unit-modulus phases, 2.45 GHz carrier, 61.44 MHz bandwidth, wideband multipath (p. 3, 9).
method: Model-free actor-critic DRL (DDPG, TD3, SAC), two hidden layers of 512 ReLU nodes, trained online by interaction in each coherence block (p. 16, 17).
data_channel: Custom simulator: Rayleigh BS-UE link, Rician BS-RIS-UE link with delayed NLoS taps, random-walk UE, random channels per episode; no dataset (p. 4, 9, 16).
test_conditions: Agents learn online inside each simulated channel block; sweeps over delayed paths, RIS size and Rician factor restart from random network seeds per point (p. 16, 19).
baselines: Non-learned: ARISE steepest descent, Random Phases, Inverse Phases (channel conjugate); learned: DDPG, TD3 and SAC compared with each other (p. 9, 17, 18).
metrics: Normalized equalization reward ηn, raw objective η (main tap power minus ISI power), pulse responses, QPSK constellations, CDFs, convergence steps, power gain (p. 5, 17, 18).
complexity: Per-step orders in Table 1: SAC O(Ntrain(2Ccritic+Cactor)), DDPG O(Ntrain(Ccritic+Cactor)), ARISE O(M(L+1)^2); DRL inference about linear in M (p. 14, 15).
q1_support: p. 4: "We model the channel fading parameters using Rician coefficients" (custom simulator with Rayleigh NLoS taps); p. 9: "in accordance with the 3GPP standard for 5G New Radio (NR)" fixes only the symbol duration and bandwidth, not the channel. No 3GPP channel model, DeepMIMO, COST 2100 or measured data.
q2_support: p. 19: "we modify the input and output dimensions of the actor and critic DNNs to correspond with each variable change"; p. 19: "random seeds for both the DNNs and the channel coefficients". Each sweep point trains new networks and the agent learns online in the tested channel, so no held-out scenario is tested.
q3_support: p. 9: "We define two baseline RIS reflection coefficient schemes for comparison"; p. 17: "SAC achieves equalization performance comparable and at times exceeding that of ARISE"; p. 18: "DDPG is trailing behind and gets stuck at local optima, often unable to achieve the performance of TD3". Non-learned: ARISE, Random and Inverse Phases; learned: standard DDPG and TD3 on the same task, compared on the equalization reward.
q4_support: p. 15: "The per-step complexities of all the algorithms are summarized in Table 1."; p. 15: "we obtain T SAC = O(Ntrain (2Ccritic + Cactor ))". Table 1 (p. 14) also lists O(M(L+1)^2) for ARISE.
q5_support: p. 17: "The networks are trained using TensorFlow Keras [54] in Python, using the Adam optimizer [68]." The channels are simulated; the paper gives no link to code or data and uses no public dataset or measured data.
notes: Included, area 3: the learned DRL agents output the RIS reflection coefficients (the equalization is done over the air by the RIS), so the function is RIS configuration and not receiver-side detection. Single antenna at both ends but with a RIS, so the single-antenna exclusion does not apply (p. 3). q3 relies on DDPG and TD3 as standard DRL algorithms applied to the same problem and on the non-learned ARISE, Random and Inverse Phases, so the reviewer should confirm it. q2 is 0: the agents learn online in each channel block, the sweeps over M, nr and kappa restart from random network seeds, and the 100-episode random-walk run (Fig. 13, p. 18) is continual online learning without a held-out test. Tables 1 to 3 and Figs. 12 to 16 were read from the PDF pages.
